summary.text: The Big Bang is a physical theory describing how the universe expanded from an early state of high density and temperature.
Its models explain the abundance of light elements, the cosmic microwave background, the redshift of galaxies and the large-scale structure of the universe.
Measurements of the expansion place the age of the universe at an estimated 13.787 billion years, and a wide range of evidence strongly favors the model.

items.prompt: In the 1960s radio astronomers found a glow that looked the same in every direction. Why did that count against the steady-state rival?

options.label: It showed galaxies were all moving toward us
It proved the universe has no age at all
It matched stars simply being born and dying forever
Its uniformity and energy curve fit a hot, dense distant past

items.explain: The radiation's uniformity and the shape of its energy curve both fit Big Bang models of high temperature and density, and by the late 1960s most cosmologists dropped the steady-state model.

items.prompt: Looking in opposite directions, the universe appears remarkably alike. Which idea within Big Bang models accounts for that?

options.label: A phase of accelerated expansion in the earliest stages
Dark energy speeding up the expansion in recent times
Gravity pulling matter together into galaxies
Dark matter holding galaxies together as they spin

items.explain: The observed uniformity is explained through cosmic inflation, a phase of accelerated expansion during the earliest stages.

items.prompt: The first stars and galaxies formed from leftovers of the young universe. What were those leftovers mostly?

options.label: Mostly carbon, with some iron and oxygen
Mostly helium, with some hydrogen and gold
Mostly hydrogen, with some helium and lithium
Equal shares of hydrogen, silicon and iron

items.explain: The primordial elements were mostly hydrogen, with some helium and lithium, and they coalesced under gravity aided by dark matter.

items.prompt: Astronomers measure the redshifts of distant exploding stars and find the expansion is speeding up. What is that attributed to?

options.label: The extra matter left by baryon asymmetry
A concept called dark energy
A reheating event after inflation ended
The pull of dark matter around galaxies

items.explain: Redshifts of supernovae indicate accelerating expansion, an observation attributed to dark energy.

items.prompt: The universe has a finite age and light has a finite speed. What does that mean for the most distant things we can see?

options.label: Every event in the past has already sent its light to Earth
Light slows down once it has crossed a certain distance
Distant objects stop emitting light after a certain age
Light from some past events has not yet had time to reach Earth

items.explain: Since the universe has a finite age, there may be past events whose light has not reached Earth, which sets a past horizon on the most distant observable objects.

items.prompt: Which puzzle do Big Bang models still leave inadequately explained?

options.label: Why matter is more abundant than antimatter
Why the microwave background looks the same everywhere
Why galaxies appear to be moving away from us
Why the early universe was mostly hydrogen

items.explain: The unequal abundances of matter and antimatter, called baryon asymmetry, remain unexplained, while the microwave background, redshift and element abundances are explained.

beats.title: Rewinding the Universe
beats.hook: Run the expansion backward and everything squeezes together.

beats.prompt: Astronomers extrapolate the universe's expansion backward in time using the known laws of physics. What do the models describe?
beats.explain: Extrapolating the expansion backward describes an extraordinarily hot and dense primordial universe.

choices.label: An extraordinarily hot and dense primordial universe
A universe of the same size and density as now
choices.feedback: The universe is expanding, so earlier it was smaller and denser.

choices.label: A cold, empty universe much like today
choices.feedback: Running expansion backward packs things closer together, which makes them hotter, not emptier.

items.label: Hubble publishes the work known as Hubble's law
The CMB is discovered by accident

right.label: Aided gravity in forming early stars and galaxies

beats.explain: Each idea plays a different part in the story from the earliest stages to today.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?

steps.text: The universe has a finite age.
Light travels at a finite speed.
So light from every past event has already reached us.
So there is no limit on the most distant objects we can observe.

beats.idea: Expansion, leftover radiation and the first elements all point back to a hot, dense start.

paragraphs.heading: What the theory says
paragraphs.text: The Big Bang is a physical theory of how the universe grew out of an early state that was very dense and very hot. Running the expansion backward with the known laws of physics leads to an extremely hot, dense early universe. Models built on this idea account for many things we observe: how common the light elements are, the cosmic microwave background (CMB), the redshifted light of galaxies, and how the universe is arranged on the largest scales. A wide range of evidence strongly favours the model, and it is now widely accepted.

paragraphs.heading: From inflation to galaxies
paragraphs.text: The original model traced the universe back toward a singularity. The modern view adds cosmic inflation, a phase of speeded-up expansion in the earliest moments, out of which the universe came in a supercooled state. A reheating event then turned the energy that powered inflation into a hot, dense plasma, which set off the hot Big Bang. As the universe expanded, it cooled enough for subatomic particles to form, and later atoms. These first elements, mostly hydrogen with some helium and lithium, were pulled together by gravity, helped by dark matter, into early stars and galaxies.

paragraphs.heading: How the idea took shape
paragraphs.text: Alexander Friedmann introduced the idea of an expanding universe in 1922, when he derived the Friedmann equations. In 1929 Edwin Hubble published the earliest observation of the expansion, now called Hubble's law: galaxies are moving away from Earth, and the farther they are, the faster they go. Working apart from both men, Georges Lemaître proposed in 1931 that the universe came from a primeval atom, which introduced the modern Big Bang idea. In 1964 the CMB was found by accident, and measurements over the next few years showed it was the same in every direction and had an energy curve that fit a hot, dense past. By the late 1960s most cosmologists were sure the rival steady-state model was wrong.

paragraphs.heading: Three working assumptions
paragraphs.text: The models rest on three main assumptions. The first is that the laws of physics hold everywhere. The second, called the cosmological principle, says the universe, viewed at large scales, is homogeneous and isotropic, meaning it looks the same in every direction wherever you stand. The third is that matter can be treated as a perfect fluid, one with no viscosity and with pressure in proportion to density. These started as postulates but have since been tested: the fine-structure constant has shifted by at most about 10⁻⁵ over much of the universe's age, and CMB temperatures confirm the cosmological principle to a level of 10⁻⁵.

paragraphs.heading: What the universe is made of
paragraphs.text: In Big Bang cosmology, the density of mass and energy decides the shape of the universe and how it changes. Putting observations together with thermodynamics and particle physics, cosmologists have traced what that density consists of across cosmic history. Today, luminous matter such as stars and planets is less than 5% of it. Dark matter accounts for 27%, and dark energy for the remaining 68%.

paragraphs.heading: Horizons in both directions
paragraphs.text: A key feature of the Big Bang picture is the presence of horizons. The universe has a finite age and light moves at a finite speed, so light from some past events may not have reached Earth yet, which limits how far away we can see. Going the other way, space is expanding and distant objects are moving off ever faster, so light sent out today may never catch up with them. That sets a future horizon, a limit on which future events we can affect. Supernova redshifts show the expansion is speeding up, which is put down to dark energy, and if that goes on there is a future horizon too.

paragraphs.heading: What is still unexplained
paragraphs.text: Some features of the observed universe are not yet well explained by the Big Bang models. These include why matter and antimatter exist in unequal amounts, known as baryon asymmetry. They also include the detailed nature of the dark matter around galaxies and where dark energy comes from.
